# Study figures — what the paper plots, and why

The statistical figures for §6 `Evaluation: User Study` of the CHI paper. Written
2026-09-06, after the analysis of the 18 analysed participants (P05-P22).

Companion documents: `user-study-design.md` (method in full), `study-registration.md`
(what was fixed in advance), `baseline-spec.md` (the three conditions).

**Everything here is generated by `Tools/build_study_figures.py`.** Never hand-edit a
generated PDF, and never let a number in the paper's prose come from anywhere but the same
script that draws the figure. Regenerate with:

```
python Tools/build_study_figures.py            # study 2, the paper's current study
python Tools/build_study_figures.py --study 1  # study 1
```

**Since 2026-09-10 the paper's figures are study 2's** (`--study 2`, the default): it reads
`Recordings/Study_02/P01..P18/responses.csv`, labels the participants as they are on disk
(study 2 had no pilots, so section 2.1's renumbering does nothing there), and writes into
`{PAPER_ROOT}/figures/`. Study 1 reads `Recordings/Study_01/P05..P22/responses.csv` with the
renumbering below. Everything else in this document applies to both studies unchanged; the
numbers quoted in the caption discussions below are study 1's.

**Two repositories, and one symbol for the other one.** **`{PAPER_ROOT}` stands for the CHI
paper repository**, currently at `F:\Research\CHI_2027___Explainable_Gaze_Patterns_for_Turn_Taking`.
It is a separate git repository, outside this one: the paper moved out of this repository's
git-ignored `Research/` tree on 2026-09-06 so that it could have version control of its own.
Any path written `{PAPER_ROOT}/...` is over there; a path without it is in this repository.
Write the symbol rather than a bare path, because `figures/` means something in both places.
Override the location with the `GAZECONTROL_PAPER_DIR` environment variable or `--out` rather
than editing the script.

The script requires `numpy`, `scipy`, `pandas`, `matplotlib` and `statsmodels`; the last is
what fits the mixed models the estimated marginal means come from, and the script fails loudly
rather than silently falling back to raw cell means if it is missing.

---

## 0. The reference paper, and what transfers from it

The house model is `Research/papers/2024-ISMAR-AgentBehaviorGeneration.pdf` (Gunawardhana et al.,
*Toward User-Aware Interactive Virtual Agents*, ISMAR 2024), the same paper
`style_guidlines.md` §9 makes the model for the section's prose. Its figure scheme is:

| | What it shows | Layout |
|---|---|---|
| Fig 8 | Aggregate ratings per question **category**, ours vs baseline | grouped bars, 95% CI whiskers |
| Fig 9 | The same broken out per **item** within each category | five stacked panels, full column height |
| Fig 10 | Objective measure 1 (gaze stability): **(a) per participant**, (b) aggregated | 15 participant pairs, then a summary pair |
| Fig 11 | Objective measure 2 (pupil diameter) | identical layout to Fig 10 |
| Fig 12, 13 | Gaze allocation heat map on the agent mesh; mutual-gaze bars | mesh renders, then bars |

The pattern is *aggregate, then per item, then per participant, once per measure.*

**Two of those four do not transfer.**

- **Fig 8 to Fig 9 has no analogue.** That split separates a question *category* from the
  *items* inside it. Our four constructs are one item each (N1, T2, A1, I1), so the split
  collapses and one panel does both jobs.
- **Figs 10 to 13 have no analogue.** All four are participant eye-tracking measures, and
  §7 of `user-study-design.md` puts participant gaze out of scope (2026-08-31). Our
  objective measures are stimulus-side instead: what the three policies generate, scored
  against the human corpus.

**One idiom transfers wholesale: Fig 10(a)'s per-participant panel** — and for us it
carries the *subjective* data rather than an eye-tracking measure, because that is where
our result lives. The paper's explanation for the null primary measure is that participants
disagreed about baseline B, and a per-participant panel is the visual form of that claim.

**Copy the layout, never the statistics.** ISMAR's Fig 10 and 11 whiskers are computed over
gaze *samples*, which is why they are hairline-thin beside an `F` of 31,591 with a partial
eta-squared of 0.000141. `style_guidlines.md` §9 names this as the first of two things not
to copy. Every interval in our figures is over participants (Figure 1) or over one
participant's five conversations (Figure 2), and never over trials pooled across people.

---

## 1. Figure 1 — subjective summary (`{PAPER_ROOT}/figures/us_ratings.pdf`)

Three panels on one full-width `figure*`. This is the Fig 8 analogue plus the primary
measure, which ISMAR has no counterpart for.

**(a) Ratings by construct.** Estimated marginal means with 95% confidence intervals for
the four constructs, three methods each, on the full 1-7 scale.

- The EMMs come from the **registered mixed model of each construct** (method and serial
  position as fixed effects, random intercepts for participant and conversation), averaged
  over serial position, so the figure plots exactly what the prose reports. Because the
  design is balanced the point estimate equals the raw cell mean; the interval does not,
  since it carries the participant and conversation variance.
- Keep the axis at the **full 1 to 7**. Cropping to the data range would make a 0.2-point
  difference on naturalness look like the same kind of thing as the 2.5-point difference on
  inclusion, which is the whole point of the figure being one panel.
- **Points with error bars, not bars.** A bar chart implies a meaningful zero, and a
  7-point Likert scale has none; ISMAR's bars start at 0 and spend two thirds of the panel
  on space no response can occupy.

**(b) Ranked naturalness.** Mean rank per method with 95% CI over the 18 participants.

- The **y-axis is inverted** so rank 1 (most natural) is at the top and better reads as
  higher, the same direction as panel (a). The axis label says `1 = most natural` because
  an inverted axis is a readability hazard and the reader needs telling once.
- One value per participant per method (their mean over the five blocks) before the
  interval is computed. This is the registered unit of analysis.

**(c) Rank distribution.** Stacked bars of the 90 blocks per method, split into first,
second and third place.

- This panel exists to make one claim visible: **baseline B is polarizing, not uniformly
  weak.** It took 26 first places *and* 41 last places. Panel (b) alone shows only that its
  mean rank is worst, which invites the wrong reading, and the paper's explanation of the
  null Friedman result depends on the distinction.

## 2. Figure 2 — per participant (`{PAPER_ROOT}/figures/us_per_participant.pdf`)

Two stacked full-width rows, the ISMAR Fig 10(a) layout: 18 participants along the x-axis,
three bars each, whiskers giving the standard error over that participant's five
conversations.

**Standard error here, not a 95% CI, and this is the only place the paper departs from
that.** Five conversations gives the t interval four degrees of freedom and a mean
half-width of 1.2 to 1.5 scale points; 21 of the 108 cells would then draw an interval
running past 7 or below 1, advertising ratings the instrument cannot produce, and sizing
the axis to fit them spends a fifth of the panel on impossible values while shrinking the
bars the panel exists to compare. **Any caption on this figure must say "standard error".**

**The bars grow from zero, so the axis starts at zero rather than at the scale floor.**
Five cells are exactly 1 (P11 on all three methods, and baseline B for four other
participants); an axis starting at 1 clips those to nothing and they read as missing data
rather than as the floor responses they are.

### 2.1 Participants are drawn as P01-P18, not P05-P22

**The analysed set is renumbered from one for publication.** The gap at the front is an
artifact of the pilot exclusion, and an axis that starts at P05 makes a reader ask where
the first four went, which is a question §6's exclusion sentence has already answered in
prose. Nothing is gained by making the figure re-raise it.

The map is **order-preserving and one-to-one**, so it loses nothing and is reversible:
display `P01` is the first entry of the analysed list, `P02` the second, and so on.
`build_study_figures.py` derives it from position rather than storing a table, so the two
cannot drift apart, and it **prints the whole mapping on every run** for exactly the case
below.

| disk | paper | disk | paper | disk | paper |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| P05 | P01 | P11 | P07 | P17 | P13 |
| P06 | P02 | P12 | P08 | P18 | P14 |
| P07 | P03 | P13 | P09 | P19 | P15 |
| P08 | P04 | P14 | P10 | P20 | P16 |
| P09 | P05 | P15 | P11 | P21 | P17 |
| P10 | P06 | P16 | P12 | P22 | P18 |

**Watch the overlap when tracing a bar back to a log.** Twelve of the eighteen display
labels also exist as disk labels and name a *different* person: the floor responder drawn
as `P11` is `Recordings/Study_01/P15/`, not `Recordings/Study_01/P11/`. Anything written about an individual
participant should say which namespace it is in. `study-registration.md`,
`user-study-design.md` and `PROGRESS.md` are all in **disk** labels, because they were
written while the sessions were being run and the filenames are what they refer to.

**(a) Inclusion (I1)** and **(b) Gaze naturalness (N1)**, in that order.

The pairing is the figure. Read together the two rows show why one hypothesis is verified
and the other is not:

- **(a) is uniform.** Our method is above baseline B for 16 of the 18 participants and
  below it for none, and the effect reproduces in all five conversations.
- **(b) is not.** Baseline B's participant means span **1.0 to 6.4** — five participants
  rate it at or above 5.5, four at or below 3.5 — against 2.6 to 5.8 for our method. This
  is the same fact the mixed models report as a participant-by-method variance component of
  1.11 to 1.88 for baseline B against 0.01 to 0.26 for baseline A, and it is far more
  legible drawn than tabulated.

**Participants stay in label order.** Sorting them by effect size would make both panels
look tidier and would misrepresent both: the point of (a) is that nearly every bar goes the
same way, and the point of (b) is that they do not.

**Bars here, points in Figure 1.** Fifty-four adjacent estimates read better as bars than as
a picket fence of dots, and unlike the summary panel the comparison being made is local
(within one participant's triple) rather than across the whole scale.

## 3. Figure 3 — generated-gaze fidelity (dropped 2026-09-06)

Planned as three panels scoring each policy against the human corpus as a reference column
(role-conditioned target proportions, dwell CDFs, shift timing around each EoT event), the
analogue of ISMAR Figs 10, 11 and 13. **Dropped, by the user's call**, and the paper's §6 no
longer promises it. The reference would have been `Research/corpora/gaze_events/gaze_events_md6.csv`,
which is the corpus our method *replays* (holding stretches between boundaries, prototypes
at them) and baseline A is *fitted to*, so the match was by construction for two of the three
policies. A figure showing that a policy sampled from a corpus resembles that corpus does not
make the method more convincing; it invites the objection instead of answering it. Only
baseline B could have been far from the reference, and its two telling numbers (no aversion,
almost no gaze at the human) are already in §6's hypotheses paragraph.

Two things learned while assessing it, kept because they outlive the figure:

- **Every participant saw the same fifteen tracks.** One arbitrary base seed per clip
  (`user-study-design.md`, clip table), baked once on 2026-08-27 to
  `Assets/DemoSegments/study_c*/gazetrack_<Condition>_seed<N>.json` and replayed to all
  eighteen; verified on the logs, P09 and P10 have identical gaze-target transition sequences
  on `study_c1` in all three conditions. Any stimulus-side measure is therefore computed
  over those fifteen tracks, on the decision grid, and the "logs exist for ten of eighteen
  participants" caveat never applies to it (P05-P08 wrote header-only agent logs from the
  `ArmTake` null read fixed 2026-09-01, P19-P22 none; that affects only analyses of the
  rendered frames).
- **If a stimulus description is ever wanted**, it is one sentence or a small table of
  per-policy aversion fraction and gaze-at-human fraction from the baked tracks, presented as
  what each version looked like, not as evidence. A genuine fidelity test would need a
  held-out group (the corpus's date-prefix `group` key, one per triad) with baseline A refitted
  and the holding bank rebuilt without it; that changes the stimulus and is a separate study.

---

## 4. Figures deliberately not drawn

- **The variance components.** A panel of the participant-by-method variance would restate
  Figure 2(b), which shows the same fact more legibly and without asking the reader to
  interpret a variance component.
- **The serial-position effect.** Real and reported (ratings rise about 0.4 points from the
  first version of a block to the second and third), but it is a sentence. The
  counterbalancing keeps it out of the method contrast, so it is a check that passed rather
  than a result.
- **A per-conversation breakdown**, the honest analogue of ISMAR's Fig 9 — five
  conversations by three methods by four constructs, showing the effect replicating. It
  belongs in supplementary material if anywhere; in the main paper it costs a full column
  to make a point the text can make in a clause.

---

## 5. Plotting conventions

Set once at the top of `Tools/build_study_figures.py`; change them there, not per figure.

- **Serif font at 7.5 pt**, matching the `acmart` body text so a figure does not read as a
  foreign object on the page.
- **Greyscale-safe encoding.** Ours is near-black, baseline A mid-grey, baseline B light
  grey, and in Figure 1 the three also carry distinct markers (circle, square, triangle) so
  the panels survive a monochrome print and a colour-blind reader alike.
- **`pdf.fonttype: 42`** (TrueType), so text in the figure stays selectable and searchable
  in the compiled PDF rather than being drawn as outlines.
- **Vector PDF output**, never PNG. The figures are line art and get scaled by the
  typesetter.
- **Full text width** (`figure*` at `\textwidth`) for both figures. Figure 1's three panels
  and Figure 2's 54 bars per row do not fit a single column legibly.
- **Width is fixed, height is the free dimension — spend height, not width.** When something
  does not fit sideways, the reflex is to steal width from a neighbouring panel, and that
  reflex is wrong: `\textwidth` is a hard budget, so every point one panel gains another
  loses, and the cost usually lands on axis labels that then collide. Figure 1(c)'s legend
  is the worked example. Three horizontal entries overflowed the axes frame; widening (c)
  at the expense of (a) immediately ran (a)'s four construct names into each other. The fix
  was to make the *figure taller* and stack that legend in one column, which costs almost no
  width, and all three panels kept the proportions their content wants.
- **Every interval is a 95% CI and the caption says so**, per `style_guidlines.md` §9, with
  the single documented exception of Figure 2's standard errors (§2 above gives the reason).
  Where the unit differs between panels, the caption names the unit for each: Figure 1(a)'s
  intervals come from the mixed models, 1(b)'s are over the 18 participants, and 2's are
  over one participant's five conversations.
- **Where a quantity is drawn as bars, the axis starts at zero**, because a bar encodes
  length from zero and a truncated baseline silently rescales every comparison. Point-and-
  interval panels have no such constraint and use the response scale directly.

---

## 6. Naming, in figures and in prose

**The item codes N1, T2, A1 and I1 never appear in the paper.** They are internal
identifiers: they key `Assets/GazeControl/Resources/Questionnaire.json`, the `item` column
of `responses.csv`, and the `CONSTRUCTS` list in the generator. Everything the reviewer
sees names the construct instead: *gaze naturalness*, *boundary gaze quality*, *mutual
engagement*, *inclusion*.

**Why, since ISMAR codes its items.** ISMAR needs `FA-1` through `FA-5` because five items
share one category and have to be told apart. We have **one item per construct**, so a code
plus a number disambiguates nothing, and it costs the reader four arbitrary tokens to
memorise. Worse, it raises a question it cannot answer: `T2` is the second boundary item
drafted, `T1` having been cut during design (`user-study-design.md` §6.2 records what was
cut and why), and `N1`, `A1` and `I1` are firsts. A reviewer reading `T2` beside three
`x1`s wonders where `T1` went. That is our design history, and it is not the reader's
problem to carry.

**What replaced the code column in Table `tab:us_items` in the paper**: which hypothesis each item
tests, `$H_{nat}$` and so on. A code is an arbitrary handle; the hypothesis is the thing a
reviewer actually wants when reading an item, and it ties the table to both the hypotheses
paragraph and the results.

**The hypothesis subscripts stay** — `$H_{rank}$`, `$H_{nat}$`, `$H_{bnd}$`, `$H_{eng}$`,
`$H_{inc}$` — and are reused verbatim in the results, which is what `style_guidlines.md`
§9 prescribes. They are mnemonic rather than arbitrary, so they cost the reader nothing.

Corollary for anyone editing §6 later: if a sentence needs to refer to one item, write
*the inclusion item* or *the naturalness item*, never `I1` or `N1`.
